planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich but sharply drained soil in full sun; unlike the drier-summer reticulata iris it was bred with, this species wants a cooler, slightly moister summer rest rather than a hard baking.

directions: Plant bulbs shallowly, about 3 to 4 inches deep, in fall in gritty, humus-rich soil that drains well but doesn't bake bone-dry over summer, since this species comes from damp Caucasus mountain meadows rather than the arid steppe that other reticulata-group irises favor. It bears bright, clear yellow flowers lightly netted with faint darker veining on short stems only a few inches tall, opening in very early spring just after the common blue reticulata iris. It is one of the two wild parents behind the muted blue-grey hybrid 'Frank Elder', prized for passing on larger flower size and an extended color range to its hybrid offspring. Leave the grassy foliage to yellow and die back naturally, and avoid letting the planting dry out completely in summer the way true desert-origin reticulatas prefer.

common_name: Hardy Red Spider Lily (Fertile Diploid Form)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck near the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; leafless flower stalks emerge in late summer to early fall, with strap-like foliage following afterward and persisting through winter.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck near the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in late summer or fall. Unlike the familiar sterile, triploid red spider lily that spread across Gulf South gardens by division alone, this diploid botanical variety from central China sets viable seed and tends to be somewhat hardier and more cold-tolerant, which is why breeders such as Wyndham Hayward used it as a parent in creating hybrids like Lycoris x haywardii. Bare stalks carry clusters of bright red, spidery, reflexed flowers well before the strap-shaped leaves appear, with foliage persisting through the cooler months before dying back by late spring. Leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since flowering improves with congestion and division interrupts bloom the following season.

common_name: White Dream Tulip (Pure White Triumph Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall, allowing several weeks of cool soil before hard freeze for strong root establishment.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. White Dream is a classic Triumph tulip with pure white, goblet-shaped flowers on sturdy, medium-height stems, blooming in mid-spring and holding up well to wind and rain compared to taller tulip classes. Its clean, unmarked white color makes it a popular choice for all-white spring displays and as a base for mixed plantings with later-flowering bulbs. As with most hybrid tulips, it is more reliable as an annual or short-lived perennial planting outside of climates with consistently cold winters and sharp summer drainage, and it is also notable as the parent of the ruffled sport 'Super Parrot'.
